> Spacing (The spacing between each iteration.)

2278.d:
Hatchbeats are endless beat generators.

After a Hatchbeat loads, click once to start the beat, and click again to hatch it. Once hatched, clicking will toggle the audio.

Hatchbeats are not drum loops. Each Hatchbeat continuously improvises bars based on its prototype. Prototypes are patterns of hits where each hit has some probability of happening in any bar. There are 3 high hat prototypes and 4 kick/snare prototypes.

Each Hatchbeat selects high hat, kick, and snare sounds from 76 possible samples which have 8736 combinations. The playback rates of these samples are modified for each Hatchbeat to create a virtually infinite number of drum kits.

Hatchbeat tempos range from 140 bpm to 200 bpm and come in several colors.

RIBBON FIELDS //GENESIS


RIBBON FIELDS //GENESIS is a series of generative projects. This is the first one in the series but also my very first one ever. This is my genesis, I hope you like it.

In RIBBON FIELDS //GENESIS, you see a delicate balance between light (colorful lines that simply move along trying to survive) and darkness (darker lines trying to erase the colored ones) moving along a flow field. I iterated a couples of times before finding the best mix between light, dark, balance but also a bit of mystery.

2332.d:
640 unique sketches of imaginary walls, inspired by the work of Norwegian architect Erling Viksjø (1910–1971) and his artist collaborators. Viksjø designed the Government Quarter in Oslo and invited artists from different disciplines to help design the facades and interiors of the buildings.

Viksjø’s aim was to “soften” modernist architecture. He invented «Natural Concrete», a type of concrete that deliberately exposes the mixed-in stones on its surface to give it warmth and a human touch. In my work, I have similar ambitions—using code instead of concrete.

The different styles of the piece are inspired by, and dedicated to some of the artists who worked together with Viksjø: Jakob Weidemann (~2%), Carl Nesjar (~18%), Odd Tandberg (~30%), and Tore Haaland (~50%).

In live mode, press ‘S’ to save an image at current resolution or ‘P’ to save a high-resolution file at 6000×6000px (this might take a while depending on your hardware).

Original artwork by Andreas Rau · Made with p5.js & glsl · Oslo, 2021

This is a GPGPU implementation of the classic "boids" algorithm by Craig Reynolds. The simulation is moving 8192 vehicles represented as asteroids that are floating around the origin of the scene. 

Collectors can control the camera angle and zoom. Besides extra controls appear if a double click is performed on the scene. 

Extra controls include:
- Alignment factor ("boids" algorithm)
- Cohesion factor ("boids" algorithm)
- Separation factor ("boids" algorithm)
- Force to center ("boids" algorithm)
- Max speed ("boids" algorithm)
- Max force ("boids" algorithm)
- Range ("boids" algorithm)
- Strength (bloom postprocessing effect)
- Radius (bloom postprocessing effect)
- Threshold (bloom postprocessing effect)

WebGL2 is the graphics API and Three.js the library.

Created and minted in Dec 2021

2387.d:
Vortice Lux: A companion piece to Vortice Umbra.

Concentric, slightly-eccentric ellipses rotate, producing phasing patterns. The ellipses are rendered with drop-shadows, with the light slowly varying over time. Vortice Lux features a light background over which patterns of light and shadow interplay.

Features:

Spacing: Wider spacing produces bolder patterns and emphasises the light and dark spaces. All sizes are equally likely.

Eccentricity: This affects the shape. An eccentricity close to one produces a subtle effect, whilst lower eccentricities emphasise the changes in the spiral.

Rotation: There are three speeds; a relatively-rapid speed, a steady, almost-default speed, and a slower, more contemplative version. The default speed is most likely.

Highlights: The drop-shadow effect is more likely to be light, producing a brighter edge to each set of ellipses. A dark-shadowed version is also available, with a probability of around a quarter.

Inversion: The default mode is a lightly-hued background.

2441.d:
The canvas is split into small squares, separated by gridlines of uniform thickness. Each square is filled with a repeating pattern of dots. Rotation is applied, and some squares are inverted.

Features:

Granularity - a larger granularity means the dots are likely to be larger. There is still a chance of small dots within a grid, but they become less likely as granularity increases.

Grid size - A simple one; the number of squares. Mid-range values are more likely.

Inverse probability - The likelihood that a particular square will be white-on-black rather than black-on-white. Equal numbers are slightly more likely.

Grid lines - These can be black, white or grey. They are most likely to be grey.

Grid spacing - The distance between individual squares.

2447.d:
Hash Effects is an introspective graphical performance that discovers its own abstract origins and morphs it into concrete forms.

The origins of these artworks lie within the transaction hash that results from minting a unique edition of the artwork. Each graphical trait in the artwork is controlled by this origin, so in essence the transaction hash is responsible for the entire artwork.

While most generative artworks hide their transaction hash in abstraction, Hash Effects shows it front and center. Each unique artwork celebrates its own transaction hash as a graphical element that morphs into various shapes over different animation scenes.

2474.d:
This artwork builds upon the annual Earth Day animations I’ve been making since 2009. The particle system was written from scratch in vanilla javascript (a single 22KB HTML/JS file). The particles are constrained to the surface of a sphere and exhibit "social interactions" from which life-like patterns emerge.

Each animation will be minted with a randomly assigned color palette, energy level, particle type, and social behavior. Over 900 basic phenotypes are possible, with countless subtleties expressed per phenotype. There are a few wild rarities waiting to be born as well...

This work evolved over a three day creative sprint with fellow algorithmic artist Canton Becker. We think the Earth deserves a blockchain that doesn't blow tons of carbon. This animation pays tribute to the climate scientists and tech innovators who are working to secure our future on this planet. To that end, 10% of all proceeds from this project will be donated to The Coalition for Rainforest Nations.

2498.d:
He gets up in the morning and he paints 200,000 strokes

There is 10% chance he will pick a white canvas and paint with black.
There is 10% chance he will pick a black canvas and paint with white.
But most likely (80% chance) he will pick a black canvas and paint with random colors.
When he picks the random colors, he will choose a pallet of 2-7 totally random colors and randomly pick one of them them every 400 strokes.
He repeats that 500 times and then he stops.
